The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Neural Language Models as Psycholinguistic Subjects: Representations of Syntactic State
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural network language models reflect incremental representations of syntactic state?
papers.core_contribution: Large LSTMs trained on large datasets can represent syntactic state comparably to an explicitly syntactic model (RNNG), and data size is crucial for learning fine-grained lexical cues to syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: All models show basic incremental syntactic state representation, but capturing fine-grained lexical cues requires large amounts of data, while coarse-grained structure can be learned with either syntactic supervision or large data.
papers.key_findings:
All tested models show basic evidence of incremental syntactic state representation (e.g., subordinate clause licensing).
Only the large LSTMs (GRNN, JRNN) and the RNNG fully capture the proper behavior of subordinate clauses (no-matrix penalty).
All models show NP/Z garden path effects, but only large LSTMs are sensitive to verb transitivity as a cue.
All models show MV/RR garden path effects, but only large LSTMs and the RNNG are sensitive to verb morphology as a cue.
The representation of syntactic state degrades with increasing intervening material in some models (GRNN and TinyLSTM).
future_direction: Using psycholinguistic methodology as a basis for more systematic tests of the linguistic competence of NLP systems.
papers.abstract: We deploy the methods of controlled psycholinguistic experimentation to shed light on the extent to which the behavior of neural network language models reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset; and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: Multilingual Probing of Deep Pre-Trained Contextual Encoders
papers.research_question: What linguistic information do multilingual pre-trained contextual encoders retain, and how does this information vary across languages, encoders, and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive multilingual evaluation of pre-trained encoders using probing tasks, revealing that recurrent architectures (ELMo) better retain lower-level linguistic information than self-attentive ones (BERT, XLM), and that cross-lingual training (XLM) leads to a loss of language-specific linguistic details.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful method for comparing encoders across languages, and the choice of encoder architecture and training objective significantly affects what linguistic information is retained, with cross-lingual models sacrificing language-specific details.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrent architectures (ELMo) retain lower-level linguistic phenomena (e.g., sentence length, word count) better than self-attentive architectures (BERT, XLM).
XLM performs worse on most probing tasks compared to BERT and ELMo, likely due to its cross-lingual training objective causing a loss of language-specific information.
For semantic tasks, the performance gap between recurrent and self-attentive architectures is smaller.
Language-specific differences exist; for example, French and Spanish perform better on subject and object number tasks due to morphological marking.
The results do not indicate that English is better represented in the multilingual models than the other languages studied.
papers.limitation:
Use of non-gold-standard dependency parses for some languages may introduce inaccuracies in the probing data.
The probing tasks are limited and do not include many truly semantic tasks.
future_direction: Designing more semantic-level probing tasks, possibly using cross-lingual semantic resources like the Parallel Meaning Bank.
Extending the evaluation to more languages and tasks.
papers.abstract: Encoders that generate representations based on context have, in recent years, benefited from adaptations that allow for pre-training on large text corpora. Earlier work on evaluating fixed-length sentence representations has included the use of ‘probing’ tasks, that use diagnostic classifiers to attempt to quantify the extent to which these encoders capture specific linguistic phenomena. The principle of probing has also resulted in extended evaluations that include relatively newer word-level pre-trained encoders. We build on probing tasks established in the literature and comprehensively evaluate and analyse – from a typological perspective amongst others – multilingual variants of existing encoders on probing datasets constructed for 6 non-English languages. Specifically, we probe each layer of a multiple monolingual RNN-based ELMo models, the transformer-based BERT’s cased and uncased multilingual variants, and a variant of BERT that uses a cross-lingual modelling scheme (XLM).

papers.title: Discourse structure interacts with reference but not syntax in neural\n language models
papers.research_question: Does discourse structure (implicit causality) influence reference and syntactic processing in neural language models, and how does this compare to human behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models learn a representational distinction for implicit causality that influences reference resolution but not syntactic attachment, while LSTM language models fail to learn such a distinction, revealing a mismatch between learned representations and behavior in language models.
papers.conclusion: Language models can learn discourse structure (implicit causality) from text, but they do not consistently use this knowledge in behavior, especially for syntactic processing, indicating limitations in how they acquire and utilize linguistic abstractions.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM language models show no influence of implicit causality on reference or syntax.
TransformerXL shows partial implicit causality representation, influencing reference but not syntax.
GPT-2 XL shows robust implicit causality effects on reference, matching human behavior, but not on syntax.
Transformers encode implicit causality in representations for both reference and syntax, but this knowledge does not affect syntactic behavior.
Both transformer models show a strong preference for local agreement in syntax, overriding discourse effects.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to unidirectional models and specific architectures, so mechanistic claims about the relationship between learned linguistic knowledge and model configurations are cautioned.
The representational similarity measure (Pearson's r) may not be optimal for capturing the relevant distinctions, especially for LSTM models.
The models may be unable to learn the syntactic operation of attachment, as suggested by the erasure of number agreement in final layers.
future_direction: Investigate the role of training objectives, such as predicting coherence relations instead of next-word prediction.
Explore the exact role of training data and model architecture in learning linguistic interactions.
Cross-linguistic studies to further understand the limitations of language models in learning syntax.
papers.abstract:
Language models (LMs) trained on large quantities of text have been claimed
to acquire abstract linguistic representations. Our work tests the robustness
of these abstractions by focusing on the ability of LMs to learn interactions
between different linguistic representations. In particular, we utilized
stimuli from psycholinguistic studies showing that humans can condition
reference (i.e. coreference resolution) and syntactic processing on the same
discourse structure (implicit causality). We compared both transformer and long
short-term memory LMs to find that, contrary to humans, implicit causality only
influences LM behavior for reference, not syntax, despite model representations
that encode the necessary discourse information. Our results further suggest
that LM behavior can contradict not only learned representations of discourse
but also syntactic agreement, pointing to shortcomings of standard language
modeling.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: Neural Networks Can Learn Patterns of Island-insensitivity in Norwegian
papers.research_question: Whether Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can learn the distribution of acceptable filler-gap dependencies and cross-linguistic differences in island constraints in Norwegian from input data.
papers.core_contribution: LSTM RNNs can learn cross-linguistic differences in island constraints (e.g., that embedded questions are not islands in Norwegian but subject and adjunct phrases are), supporting the claim that such constraints can be induced from input patterns without domain-specific learning biases.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that RNNs can learn cross-linguistic differences in island constraints from input, leading to a reassessment of the importance of domain-specific learning biases in acquiring such constraints.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM RNNs learn that filler-gap dependencies (FGDs) are unbounded in Norwegian.
LSTM RNNs show reduced filler effects inside subject islands in Norwegian, indicating sensitivity to this constraint.
LSTM RNNs show reduced filler effects inside temporal adjunct islands in Norwegian.
LSTM RNNs treat embedded questions similarly to declarative complements in Norwegian, suggesting they are not islands.
LSTM RNNs exhibit different patterns for whether-islands in English and Norwegian, indicating learning from language-specific input.
papers.limitation:
In Experiment 4, filled gap effects were not robust in subject position, which might be due to that-trace effects or low frequency of embedded subject gaps in training data.
The models might not fully treat adjuncts as islands, as filler effects were not zero in the adjunct island condition.
It is unknown whether the model's active gap-filling behavior mirrors human behavior for Norwegian.
It cannot be verified whether the models learned from direct evidence of FGDs into embedded questions or indirectly.
future_direction: Future work should test the alignment between the model’s performance and human behavior.
Future work using this paradigm should consider the dissociation between filled gap effects and unlicensed gap effects when interpreting results.
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can capture abstract generalizations about filler-gap dependencies (FGDs) in English and so-called island constraints on their distribution (Wilcox et al., 2018; 2021). These results have been interpreted as evidence that it is possible, in principle, to induce complex syntactic knowledge from the input without domain-specific learning biases. However, the English results alone do not establish that island constraints were induced from distributional properties of the training data instead of simply reflecting architectural limitations independent of the input to the models. We address this concern by investigating whether such models can learn the distribution of acceptable FGDs in Norwegian, a language that is sensitive to fewer islands than English (Christensen, 1982). Results from five experiments show that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) RNNs can (i) learn that Norwegian FGD formation is unbounded, (ii) recover the island status of temporal adjunct and subject islands, and (iii) learn that Norwegian, unlike English, permits FGDs into two types of embedded questions. The fact that LSTM RNNs can learn cross-linguistic differences in island facts therefore strengthens the claim that RNN language models can induce the constraints from patterns in the input.

papers.title: Probing for Referential Information in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the language model capture referential information beneficial for resolving pronominal anaphora in English?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a methodology to probe for referential information in language models and finds that models capture referential aspects to some extent, with Transformers outperforming LSTMs.
papers.conclusion: Language models capture grammatical information well and some referential information, with Transformers better than LSTMs; future work should investigate the origins of these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Language models capture morphosyntactic facts about anaphora, such as agreement in gender and number.
Models also encode some semantico-referential information, though they are much better at grammar.
Transformers outperform LSTMs in all analyses, with particular better semantico-referential abilities.
Models are sensitive to distractors but not completely fooled; accuracy decreases gracefully with more distractors.
Models show limited ability to distinguish mentions of the same entity across a document, hampered by recency bias.
papers.limitation: The Transformer model is slightly larger than the LSTM (151M vs 126M parameters), which should be kept in mind when comparing results.
future_direction: Investigate where these primitive referential abilities stem from and how they can be fostered in future architectures and training setups.
Test other architectures, like CNN-based LMs and LSTMs with attention, to provide additional insights.
papers.abstract: Language models keep track of complex linguistic information about the preceding context -including, e.g., syntactic relations in a sentence. We investigate whether they also capture information beneficial for resolving pronominal anaphora in English. We analyze two state of the art models with LSTM and Transformer architectures, respectively, using probe tasks on a coreference annotated corpus.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: LINSPECTOR: Multilingual Probing Tasks for Word Representations
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate word representation models in a multilingual setting to understand what linguistic features they capture and how this correlates with downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LINSPECTOR, a set of multilingual probing tasks and an evaluation suite for word representations, and shows that probing task performance correlates with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the introduced probing tasks and the LINSPECTOR framework are effective for evaluating word representations in multiple languages and that they correlate with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.key_findings:
Probing tasks can be used to evaluate word embeddings in multiple languages and show significant positive correlation with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
All embedding models achieved their lowest score for CharacterBin, a task that requires predicting the number of characters.
D-ELMo achieves the highest scores in probing for all language-test pairs, generally followed by fastText and GloVe-BPE.
Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
The probing tasks can be used to explore word embeddings or black-box neural models for linguistic cues in a multilingual setting.
papers.limitation: Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
future_direction: Extend probing tasks to more languages and include more linguistic phenomena.
Investigate the use of probing tasks for model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Despite an ever-growing number of word representation models introduced for a large number of languages, there is a lack of a standardized technique to provide insights into what is captured by these models. Such insights would help the community to get an estimate of the downstream task performance, as well as to design more informed neural architectures, while avoiding extensive experimentation that requires substantial computational resources not all researchers have access to. A recent development in NLP is to use simple classification tasks, also called probing tasks, that test for a single linguistic feature such as part-of-speech. Existing studies mostly focus on exploring the linguistic information encoded by the continuous representations of English text. However, from a typological perspective the morphologically poor English is rather an outlier: The information encoded by the word order and function words in English is often stored on a subword, morphological level in other languages. To address this, we introduce 15 type-level probing tasks such as case marking, possession, word length, morphological tag count, and pseudoword identification for 24 languages. We present a reusable methodology for creation and evaluation of such tests in a multilingual setting, which is challenging because of a lack of resources, lower quality of tools, and differences among languages. We then present experiments on several diverse multilingual word embedding models, in which we relate the probing task performance for a diverse set of languages to a range of five classic NLP tasks: POS-tagging, dependency parsing, semantic role labeling, named entity recognition, and natural language inference. We find that a number of probing tests have significantly high positive correlation to the downstream tasks, especially for morphologically rich languages. We show that our tests can be used to explore word embeddings or black-box neural models for linguistic cues in a multilingual setting. We release the probing data sets and the evaluation suite LINSPECTOR with https://github.com/UKPLab/linspector .

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Assessing the Capacity of Transformer to Abstract Syntactic Representations: A Contrastive Analysis Based on Long-distance Agreement
papers.research_question: Do transformers encode the same abstract structure for subject-verb and object-past participle agreements, or do they use distinct mechanisms consistent with linguistic theory?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers handle subject-verb and object-past participle agreements using distinct mechanisms that are consistent with their linguistic modeling, and they base predictions on linguistically motivated cues.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of abstracting syntactic representations and their internal mechanisms reflect the linguistic distinctions between subject-verb and object-past participle agreements.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve high accuracy on both agreement tasks, but performance decreases with task difficulty.
Probing shows that number information is encoded locally in the context between cue and target.
Causal intervention reveals that the relative pronoun 'que' is critical for object-past participle agreement but not for subject-verb agreement, indicating distinct mechanisms.
Transformers are able to abstract away from lexical confounds, as shown by performance on nonce datasets.
The models' predictions are based on cues that align with French grammar rules.
papers.limitation:
Probing only reveals correlations and does not guarantee that the encoded information is used by the model.
The causal intervention by masking tokens in attention does not completely remove indirect information flow.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other linguistic phenomena and languages.
Design new probes supported by causal analysis.
papers.abstract: The long-distance agreement, evidence for syntactic structure, is increasingly used to assess the syntactic generalization of Neural Language Models. Much work has shown that transformers are capable of high accuracy in varied agreement tasks, but the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior are still not well understood. To better understand transformers' internal working, this work contrasts how they handle two superficially similar but theoretically distinct agreement phenomena: subject-verb and object-past participle agreement in French. Using probing and counterfactual analysis methods, our experiments show that i) the agreement task suffers from several confounders which partially question the conclusions drawn so far and ii) transformers handle subject-verb and object-past participle agreements in a way that is consistent with their modeling in theoretical linguistics.

papers.title: Finding Universal Grammatical Relations in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: To what extent does Multilingual BERT learn a cross-lingual representation of syntactic structure? Does mBERT learn universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations; its syntactic subspaces are shared across languages and capture dependency clusters that largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, indicating the model induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations and induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision, which largely agree with the dependency labels of Universal Dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
The structural probe recovers syntactic tree distances in multiple languages from mBERT representations.
The syntactic subspaces are shared across languages, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of syntactic information.
mBERT represents dependency clusters that largely overlap with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, showing it learns universal grammatical relations.
The cross-lingual syntactic subspace is a small part (approx. 32-128 dimensions) of the overall 768-dimensional representation.
Transfer probe performance is substantially correlated with subspace similarity across languages.
papers.limitation:
Cannot tease apart whether transfer performance is caused by subword overlap or by a more fundamental sharing of parameters.
Only conduct a qualitative study in the unsupervised emergence of dependency labels via t-SNE; future work could extend to quantitative results.
Acknowledge issues in interpreting t-SNE plots.
Methods cannot support causal implications for the decisions made by the model.
future_direction: Explore other multilingual models like XLM and XLM-RoBERTa.
Attempt to understand the extent to which the discovered properties have causal implications for the model's decisions.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found evidence that Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a transformer-based multilingual masked language model, is capable of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, suggesting that some aspects of its representations are shared cross-lingually. To better understand this overlap, we extend recent work on finding syntactic trees in neural networks' internal representations to the multilingual setting. We show that subspaces of mBERT representations recover syntactic tree distances in languages other than English, and that these subspaces are approximately shared across languages. Motivated by these results, we present an unsupervised analysis method that provides evidence mBERT learns representations of syntactic dependency labels, in the form of clusters which largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy. This evidence suggests that even without explicit supervision, multilingual masked language models learn certain linguistic universals.

papers.title: Counterfactually Probing Language Identity in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is language identity encoded and used in multilingual models, and can counterfactual probing be used to causally manipulate this identity in embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Language identity is linearly encoded in contextual token embeddings of multilingual models and can be causally manipulated via counterfactual probing to affect the language of generated tokens, but not specifically to boost translation-equivalent words, providing evidence for both language-specific and language-general components.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R contain both language-specific and language-general components, and counterfactual probing methods like AlterRep can be fruitfully applied to analyze and manipulate language identity in these models.
papers.key_findings:
Pushing token embeddings towards a target language systematically increases the probability of words from that language in masked language modeling.
Pushing embeddings away from the template language decreases the probability of words from that language.
The intervention does not specifically boost translation-equivalent words more than random words from the target language.
Pushing embeddings in the same direction as the template language has minimal effect on target word probability but increases the overall prior for that language.
The method is robust to both monolingual and synthetic code-mixed training data.
papers.limitation:
INLP extracts only linearly extractable information; more complex non-linear methods might be needed to manipulate non-linearly encoded properties.
The AlterRep procedure is sensitive to parameters like α and the number of INLP iterations, and choosing them is tricky.
The results do not demonstrate practical utility, such as for machine translation.
The work carries the general risks associated with large language models, including environmental impacts.
future_direction: Use the method to explore linguistic typology in multilingual model space.
Apply more complex non-linear erasure methods, such as those proposed by Ravfogel et al. (2022).
Translate the findings into practical applications like machine translation.
papers.abstract: Techniques in causal analysis of language models illuminate how linguistic information is organized in LLMs. We use one such technique, AlterRep, a method of counterfactual probing, to explore the internal structure of multilingual models (mBERT and XLM-R). We train a linear classifier on a binary language identity task, to classify tokens between Language X and Language Y. Applying a counterfactual probing procedure, we use the classifier weights to project the embeddings into the null space and push the resulting embeddings either in the direction of Language X or Language Y. Then we evaluate on a masked language modeling task. We find that, given a template in Language X, pushing towards Language Y systematically increases the probability of Language Y words, above and beyond a third-party control language. But it does not specifically push the model towards translation-equivalent words in Language Y. Pushing towards Language X (the same direction as the template) has a minimal effect, but somewhat degrades these models. Overall, we take these results as further evidence of the rich structure of massive multilingual language models, which include both a language-specific and language-general component. And we show that counterfactual probing can be fruitfully applied to multilingual models.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Understanding Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer in Multilingual Recurrent Neural Networks.
papers.research_question: Does exposure to a related language (L1) improve implicit syntactic knowledge in a target language (L2) within multilingual neural networks? Do these networks induce a common representation space with shared syntactic categories?
papers.core_contribution: Cross-lingual syntactic transfer in multilingual neural networks is limited and inconsistent, and optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.
papers.conclusion: Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge is limited and dependent on language pairs, and modern multilingual neural networks are still far from acquiring a true interlingua.
papers.key_findings:
Exposing a model to a related language does not always improve grammatical knowledge in the target language; in some cases, it causes negative interference.
Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge (e.g., long-range agreement in nonce sentences) is very limited and strongly dependent on the specific source-target language pair.
Part-of-speech categories are shared to a moderate extent across languages in the models, but dependency categories are not shared at all.
Language relatedness is the most determining factor for both word embedding alignment and part-of-speech transfer.
Scaling from two to nine input languages improves part-of-speech transfer among related languages but worsens it between unrelated languages.
papers.limitation:
Transfer of syntactic knowledge is limited and inconsistent, with negative interference observed in some language pairs (e.g., French to Italian).
Syntactic knowledge transfer within the models is shallow, with dependency categories not shared across languages.
papers.abstract: It is now established that modern neural language models can be successfully trained on multiple languages simultaneously without changes to the underlying architecture. But what kind of knowledge is really shared among languages within these models? Does multilingual training mostly lead to an alignment of the lexical representation spaces or does it also enable the sharing of purely grammatical knowledge? In this paper we dissect different forms of cross-lingual transfer and look for its most determining factors, using a variety of models and probing tasks. We find that exposing our LMs to a related language does not always increase grammatical knowledge in the target language, and that optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.

papers.title: Learning Music Helps You Read: Using Transfer to Study Linguistic Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: What kinds of abstract structural features do neural language models encode, and can these features be transferred to improve performance on natural language tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces TILT, a transfer learning method to analyze structural inductive biases in language models, and finds that LSTMs can transfer structural knowledge from non-linguistic data (music, code) and artificial languages to natural language, with transfer between human languages correlating with syntactic typological similarity.
papers.conclusion: LSTMs learn generalizable structural representations from various structured data, which can be transferred to model natural language; simple structural biases like head-dependent pairing are sufficient for this transfer, challenging the centrality of recursion.
papers.key_findings:
Training on non-linguistic structured data (MIDI music or Java code) improves zero-shot perplexity on Spanish compared to random baselines, indicating transfer of generalizable structural features.
Training on artificial languages with either hierarchical (nested) or flat (paired) token structure leads to similar substantial gains in modeling natural language, suggesting hierarchical recursion is not necessary for useful structural transfer.
Zero-shot transfer performance between natural languages is highly correlated with typological syntactic similarity (WALS-syntax distance), even with zero vocabulary overlap.
Pretraining on a Zipfian random distribution provides minor improvement over a uniform random distribution, but far less than any structured data, indicating vocabulary distribution alone is insufficient for strong transfer.
papers.limitation:
The results are specific to LSTMs and may not generalize to Transformer architectures.
The typological distance metric (WALS-syntax) is based on only 49 features and may not be a perfectly accurate distance metric.
future_direction: Test if the results hold on Transformer architectures.
Ablate specific structural features by creating hypothetical languages that differ in single grammatical features.
Test with structured data that's completely unrelated to language, such as images.
papers.abstract: We propose transfer learning as a method for analyzing the encoding of grammatical structure in neural language models. We train LSTMs on non-linguistic data and evaluate their performance on natural language to assess which kinds of data induce generalizable structural features that LSTMs can use for natural language. We find that training on nonlinguistic data with latent structure (MIDI music or Java code) improves test performance on natural language, despite no overlap in surface form or vocabulary. To pinpoint the kinds of abstract structure that models may be encoding to lead to this improvement, we run similar experiments with two artificial parentheses languages: one which has a hierarchical recursive structure, and a control which has paired tokens but no recursion. Surprisingly, training a model on either of these artificial languages leads to the same substantial gains when testing on natural language. Further experiments on transfer between natural languages controlling for vocabulary overlap show that zeroshot performance on a test language is highly correlated with typological syntactic similarity to the training language, suggesting that representations induced by pre-training correspond to the cross-linguistic syntactic properties. Our results provide insights into the ways that neural models represent abstract syntactic structure, and also about the kind of structural inductive biases which allow for natural language acquisition.

papers.title: Attribution Analysis of Grammatical Dependencies in LSTMs
papers.research_question: Does the LSTM language model capture grammatical dependencies (subject-verb agreement) by using spurious correlations or by actually matching verbs with their subjects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LSTM language models enforce subject-verb agreement by identifying the subject noun, not by relying on spurious correlations, as demonstrated through layer-wise relevance propagation attribution analysis.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM language model enforces subject-verb agreement in an interpretable manner, and its success on the agreement task is not due to Clever Hans behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model prediction accuracy on subject-verb agreement is positively correlated with its ability to assign higher relevance scores to the subject noun (N1) compared to other nouns (N2).
Determiners (The/the) adjust the magnitude and sometimes direction of the relevance introduced by nouns.
Polysemous verbs (like 'like') can bias the model and cause prediction errors.
For coordinated verb constructions (SVP and LVP), the model uses an alternative strategy that relies on verb coordination rather than solely identifying the subject.
The model fails on object relative clauses (ORC) and likely relies on Clever Hans behavior for that construction.
papers.limitation:
The work does not show that LSTMs can infer stack-like representations of hierarchical syntactic structure or memory-bounded approximations thereof.
The TSE templates are simple in terms of embedding depth and dependency length, limiting the complexity of the syntactic structures evaluated.
future_direction: Exploring whether LSTMs can infer hierarchical syntactic structure and handle more complex syntactic constructions.
papers.abstract: LSTM language models have been shown to capture syntax-sensitive grammatical dependencies such as subject-verb agreement with a high degree of accuracy (Linzen et al., 2016, inter alia). However, questions remain regarding whether they do so using spurious correlations, or whether they are truly able to match verbs with their subjects. This paper argues for the latter hypothesis. Using layer-wise relevance propagation (Bach et al., 2015), a technique that quantifies the contributions of input features to model behavior, we show that LSTM performance on number agreement is directly correlated with the model's ability to distinguish subjects from other nouns. Our results suggest that LSTM language models are able to infer robust representations of syntactic dependencies.
