papers.title: The Grammar of Transformers: A Systematic Review of Interpretability Research on Syntactic Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What do Transformer-based language models (TLMs) learn about syntax from the language modeling task?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic review of 337 articles on syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models, identifying an over-focus on English and BERT, and finding that TLMs capture form-oriented syntactic phenomena well but perform more variably on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface.
papers.conclusion: The review reveals a rich but heterogeneous landscape in syntactic interpretability research, with tentative evidence that formal syntax is easier for models than the syntax-semantics interface, and highlights the need for broader empirical scope and better data reporting.
papers.key_findings:
There is an over-focus on a single language (English) and a single model (BERT) in the literature.
TLMs perform better on formal syntactic phenomena (e.g., agreement) than on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface (e.g., binding).
The field uses a balanced variety of interpretability methods (behavioral, mechanistic, probing), but probing has declined in recent years.
Multilingual and typological aspects of syntax are underexplored.
BLiMP benchmark scores show that model performance scales with training data size and that bidirectional models tend to outperform causal models for given data sizes.
future_direction: Reporting complete data in studies.
Better aligning theoretical constructs and methods across studies.
Increasing the use of mechanistic methods.
Broadening the empirical scope regarding languages and linguistic phenomena.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic review of 337 articles evaluating the syntactic abilities of Transformer-based language models, reporting on 1,015 model results from a range of syntactic phenomena and interpretability methods. Our analysis shows that the state of the art presents a healthy variety of methods and data, but an over-focus on a single language (English), a single model (BERT), and phenomena that are easy to get at (like part of speech and agreement). Results also suggest that TLMs capture these form-oriented phenomena well, but show more variable and weaker performance on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface, like binding or filler-gap dependencies. We provide recommendations for future work, in particular reporting complete data, better aligning theoretical constructs and methods across studies, increasing the use of mechanistic methods, and broadening the empirical scope regarding languages and linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: Studying the Inductive Biases of RNNs with Synthetic Variations of Natural Languages
papers.research_question: How do typological properties such as word order and morphological case marking affect the ability of neural sequence models to acquire the syntax of a language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for generating synthetic languages by parametrically modifying parsed corpora to study the inductive biases of RNNs, and uses it to show that RNNs have a recency bias, that polypersonal agreement improves performance, and that overt case marking facilitates agreement prediction.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methodology is effective for studying grammatical inductive biases of RNNs, and the findings reveal that RNNs exhibit a recency bias, benefit from multitask agreement prediction, and are aided by case marking.
papers.key_findings:
Performance was higher in subject-verb-object order (SVO) than in subject-object-verb order (SOV), suggesting that RNNs have a recency bias.
Predicting agreement with both subject and object (polypersonal agreement) improves over predicting each separately, suggesting that underlying syntactic knowledge transfers across tasks.
Overt morphological case makes agreement prediction significantly easier, regardless of word order.
papers.limitation:
The reordering manipulation is limited to core elements (subjects, objects, and verbs) and does not consider word order inside other types of phrases.
The synthetic languages are simpler than natural languages because word order is completely fixed or fully flexible, while natural languages often have more complex and varied word order patterns.
future_direction: Exploring whether consistent reordering across phrase categories (head directionality parameter) improves model performance.
Conducting human experiments based on the agreement prediction task to compare human and RNN learning.
papers.abstract: How do typological properties such as word order and morphological case marking affect the ability of neural sequence models to acquire the syntax of a language? Cross-linguistic comparisons of RNNs' syntactic performance (e.g., on subject-verb agreement prediction) are complicated by the fact that any two languages differ in multiple typological properties, as well as by differences in training corpus. We propose a paradigm that addresses these issues: we create synthetic versions of English, which differ from English in one or more typological parameters, and generate corpora for those languages based on a parsed English corpus. We report a series of experiments in which RNNs were trained to predict agreement features for verbs in each of those synthetic languages. Among other findings, (1) performance was higher in subject-verb-object order (as in English) than in subject-object-verb order (as in Japanese), suggesting that RNNs have a recency bias; (2) predicting agreement with both subject and object (polypersonal agreement) improves over predicting each separately, suggesting that underlying syntactic knowledge transfers across the two tasks; and (3) overt morphological case makes agreement prediction significantly easier, regardless of word order.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
papers.research_question: What specific linguistic features does BERT learn from unlabeled data, as revealed by its attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads capture syntactic and coreference information, and proposes methods for analyzing attention mechanisms to reveal this linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps contain substantial linguistic knowledge and complement other model analysis techniques, and should be part of the toolkit for understanding what neural networks learn about language.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads exhibit common patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence.
Certain attention heads specialize to specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, determiners) with high accuracy.
One attention head performs well at coreference resolution.
An attention-based probing classifier achieves 77 UAS on dependency parsing, showing BERT's attention captures substantial syntactic information.
Attention heads in the same layer tend to behave similarly.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

papers.title: Derivational Probing: Unveiling the Layer-wise Derivation of Syntactic Structures in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are syntactic structures (micro- and macro-syntactic) constructed across the layers of neural language models? Does the derivation follow a bottom-up, top-down, or parallel pattern?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Derivational Probing, a method combining structural probing with an expected layer metric to trace the layer-wise construction of syntactic structures, revealing a bottom-up derivation in BERT where micro-syntactic structures form first and are integrated into macro-syntactic structures later.
papers.conclusion: Derivational Probing reveals that BERT constructs syntactic structures in a bottom-up manner, offering new insights into the internal mechanisms of neural language models and highlighting the importance of examining layer-wise structural formation for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
BERT models exhibit a bottom-up derivation: micro-syntactic structures (e.g., subject/object phrases) emerge in lower layers and are gradually integrated into a coherent macro-syntactic structure in higher layers.
The timing of macro-syntactic structure construction is critical for downstream performance; forming it too early (BERT-base) or too late (BERT-large) can lead to errors in tasks like subject-verb agreement.
GPT-2 models show a more parallel derivation pattern, with micro- and macro-syntactic structures emerging at similar layers, in contrast to BERT's bottom-up pattern.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on only two neural language models (BERT-base and BERT-large), and it is unclear whether similar results would be obtained for larger models or other architectural variants.
The study focused solely on English data; it is uncertain whether similar layer-wise syntactic structure construction patterns would be observed in other languages.
Semantic cues may influence the results of syntactic probes, and the study does not fully account for these potential semantic confounds.
The method relies on dependency parsing and may not be directly applicable to other grammatical theories or parsing approaches that involve non-terminal symbols, such as constituency grammar.
future_direction: Incorporating multilingual probes to determine whether the observed syntactic structures generalize beyond English.
Exploring incremental parsing strategies in autoregressive language models as an alternative to non-incremental derivation processes across layers.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that neural language models encode syntactic structures in their internal representations, yet the derivations by which these structures are constructed across layers remain poorly understood.In this paper, we propose Derivational Probing to investigate how micro-syntactic structures (e.g., subject noun phrases) and macro-syntactic structures (e.g., the relationship between the root verbs and their direct dependents) are constructed as word embeddings propagate upward across layers.Our experiments on BERT reveal a clear bottom-up derivation: micro-syntactic structures emerge in lower layers and are gradually integrated into a coherent macro-syntactic structure in higher layers.Furthermore, a targeted evaluation on subject-verb number agreement shows that the timing of constructing macro-syntactic structures is critical for downstream performance, suggesting an optimal timing for integrating global syntactic information.https://github.com/osekilab/ derivational-probing

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: When Does Syntax Mediate Neural Language Model Performance? Evidence from Dropout Probes
papers.research_question: When do language models use syntactic information causally? How can we design probes to avoid false negatives due to redundant encodings of syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dropout probes, a new neural probing architecture that encourages probes to use all relevant representations of syntax in model embeddings, enabling better causal analysis and performance improvement via syntactic information injection.
papers.conclusion: Dropout probes are effective for causal analysis of language models and can be used to improve model performance by injecting syntactic information, but further work is needed to extend the approach.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode syntactic information redundantly in their embeddings.
Dropout probes reveal causal use of syntactic representations in QA models where prior methods did not.
Injecting syntactic information at test time can improve QA model performance on syntactically challenging tasks.
NLI models do not show causal use of syntax even with dropout probes.
Dropout probes can boost model performance without retraining.
papers.limitation:
Systematic evaluation of models for many layers, multiple probes, and many counterfactuals is computationally challenging.
The transparency benefits require access to the internals of the pretrained model.
The technique is limited to diagnosis of existing models and does not train models to respond appropriately to interventions.
future_direction: Studying pretrained models beyond those considered in this work.
Further research into redundancy in embeddings.
More investigation into inserting symbolic knowledge into neural representations.
New methods for training models to respond appropriately to interventions.
papers.abstract: Recent causal probing literature reveals when language models and syntactic probes use similar representations. Such techniques may yield "false negative" causality results: models may use representations of syntax, but probes may have learned to use redundant encodings of the same syntactic information. We demonstrate that models do encode syntactic information redundantly and introduce a new probe design that guides probes to consider all syntactic information present in embeddings. Using these probes, we find evidence for the use of syntax in models where prior methods did not, allowing us to boost model performance by injecting syntactic information into representations.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Understanding Syntax in Large Language Models: Successes and Limitations
papers.research_question: How accurately can LLMs handle published examples of complex syntactic phenomena, as described in linguistic theories?
papers.core_contribution: This study evaluates the syntactic competence of LLMs, finding that while they handle simple constructions well, they struggle with complex hierarchical dependencies, highlighting the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles.
papers.conclusion: LLMs demonstrate competence in simple syntax but struggle with complex structures, indicating a gap between surface fluency and deep syntactic competence, necessitating hybrid approaches for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit high success rates for simple relative clauses and basic wh-movement, but performance declines with increased complexity.
Center-embedding poses significant challenges, with success rates dropping to around 50% for deeply embedded structures.
Errors include truncation of sentences, unresolved syntactic dependencies, and semantic incoherence in complex cases.
LLMs rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than deep generative syntactic principles.
The limitations suggest that current LLMs lack robust internal representations of hierarchical syntax.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relied exclusively on examples from English linguistic literature, not capturing syntactic diversity across languages.
The evaluation focused only on relative clauses, wh-movement, and center-embedding, without exploring broader syntactic constructs.
The study was limited to publicly available LLMs like GPT-4 and BERT, without considering effects of model size, architecture, or training data.
The evaluation did not delve into underlying representations or mechanisms of the models.
future_direction: Integrating explicit syntactic theory into neural architectures, such as the Minimalist Program or dependency grammar.
Conducting cross-linguistic comparisons to evaluate LLMs' syntactic competence across different languages.
Designing more linguistically focused benchmarks based on theoretical constructs like syntactic islands or scope ambiguity.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to process complex syntactic phenomena, including relative clauses, wh-movement, and center- embedding. By analyzing examples derived from linguistic literature, the study highlights both the strengths and limitations of LLMs in handling syntax. The results reveal that while LLMs exhibit competence in simpler syntactic constructions, they struggle with deeper hierarchical dependencies and abstract syntactic constraints. The study underscores the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles into LLM architectures to bridge the gap between surface-level fluency and generative linguistic competence.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: A Shared Geometry of Difficulty in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether problem-difficulty representations in multilingual LLMs are language-specific or shared across languages, and how they are encoded depth-dependently.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode problem difficulty in a depth-dependent manner: early layers form a language-agnostic representation that supports cross-lingual transfer, while deeper layers refine it into language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form a language-agnostic estimate of difficulty in early layers before specializing it to individual languages in deeper layers, indicating a shared geometry of difficulty across languages.
papers.key_findings:
Difficulty is linearly decodable from both shallow (early) and deep (later) transformer layers.
Probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages than those trained on deep representations.
Probes trained on deep representations achieve higher accuracy within the same language but generalize poorly across languages.
There is a trade-off between cross-lingual generalization and language-specific accuracy, with optimal layers differing for same-language vs. cross-lingual evaluation.
This depth-dependent organization of difficulty representations is consistent across multiple LLM architectures and scales.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is confined to mathematical problem solving using the AMC subset of Easy2Hard, so it is unclear if findings extend to other domains.
Empirical evaluation is limited to a small set of instruction-tuned, decoder-only language models.
Conclusions are based exclusively on probing analyses without causal evidence for the role of difficulty signals in inference.
future_direction: Whether difficulty-based interventions learned in one language transfer to other languages.
papers.abstract: Predicting problem-difficulty in large language models (LLMs) refers to estimating how difficult a task is according to the model itself, typically by training linear probes on its internal representations. In this work, we study the multilingual geometry of problem-difficulty in LLMs by training linear probes using the AMC subset of the Easy2Hard benchmark, translated into 21 languages. We found that difficulty-related signals emerge at two distinct stages of the model internals, corresponding to shallow (early-layers) and deep (later-layers) internal representations, that exhibit functionally different behaviors. Probes trained on deep representations achieve high accuracy when evaluated on the same language but exhibit poor cross-lingual generalization. In contrast, probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages, despite achieving lower within-language performance. Together, these results suggest that LLMs first form a language-agnostic representation of problem difficulty, which subsequently becomes language-specific. This closely aligns with existing findings in LLM interpretability showing that models tend to operate in an abstract conceptual space before producing language-specific outputs. We demonstrate that this two-stage representational process extends beyond semantic content to high-level meta-cognitive properties such as problem-difficulty estimation.

papers.title: Influence Paths for Characterizing Subject-Verb Number Agreement in LSTM Language Models
papers.research_question: Does an LSTM language model learn structural features of natural languages such as subject-verb number agreement, and how does it handle this concept?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces influence paths, a method to decompose the influence of a concept (e.g., subject number) on an output (e.g., verb number) into paths across gates and neurons of an LSTM, showing that subject-verb agreement is concentrated in a primary path and specific neurons.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM language model handles subject-verb number agreement in a general and localized manner, with a primary path and specific neurons responsible, and errors arise from competing influences rather than lack of structural capability.
papers.key_findings:
The same primary path carries the largest positive attribution for subject-verb number agreement across all contexts.
Two specific neurons (125 and 337 in the second layer) are consistently the most influential for number agreement.
Attractors (intervening nouns of opposite number) contribute negative attribution along the same primary path, while helpful nouns contribute positive attribution.
Model compression experiments show that the primary path accounts for most of the subject number agreement concept.
The primary path remains dominant even in the presence of attractors, indicating that errors are due to attractor influence rather than lack of concept.
papers.limitation: The analysis is based on datasets with limited context size, and the number of paths grows exponentially with context size, which may limit scalability to longer contexts.
future_direction: Investigate longer contexts and the diminishing dominance of the primary path.
Expand the method to more complicated sentences with clausal structures or other syntactic/semantic signals like coreference or gender agreement.
papers.abstract: LSTM-based recurrent neural networks are the state-of-the-art for many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Despite their performance, it is unclear whether, or how, LSTMs learn structural features of natural languages such as subject-verb number agreement in English. Lacking this understanding, the generality of LSTM performance on this task and their suitability for related tasks remains uncertain. Further, errors cannot be properly attributed to a lack of structural capability, training data omissions, or other exceptional faults. We introduce *influence paths*, a causal account of structural properties as carried by paths across gates and neurons of a recurrent neural network. The approach refines the notion of influence (the subject's grammatical number has influence on the grammatical number of the subsequent verb) into a set of gate or neuron-level paths. The set localizes and segments the concept (e.g., subject-verb agreement), its constituent elements (e.g., the subject), and related or interfering elements (e.g., attractors). We exemplify the methodology on a widely-studied multi-layer LSTM language model, demonstrating its accounting for subject-verb number agreement. The results offer both a finer and a more complete view of an LSTM's handling of this structural aspect of the English language than prior results based on diagnostic classifiers and ablation.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Language Models Learn POS First
papers.research_question: How and when are linguistic structures, such as part-of-speech tagging and global topic information, acquired during the training of language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that during training, language models acquire part-of-speech tagging early and global topic information continuously, using methods like gradient concentration and SVCCA.
papers.conclusion: Early training focuses on learning part-of-speech syntax for initial performance, while later training shifts to refining global topic representations for further gains.
papers.key_findings:
Frequent words have more concentrated gradients, and concentration increases over time during training.
Closed POS classes (e.g., pronouns, prepositions) show early concentration stabilization, while open classes (e.g., nouns, verbs) continue to become more concentrated.
Part-of-speech tagging is learned early in training, with representation peaking before the first optimizer step size rescale.
Global topic information is learned continuously throughout training, with representation increasing over time.
future_direction: Develop ways of interpreting syntactic structures during training.
papers.abstract: A glut of recent research shows that language models capture linguistic structure. Such work answers the question of whether a model represents linguistic structure. But how and when are these structures acquired? Rather than treating the training process itself as a black box, we investigate how representations of linguistic structure are learned over time. In particular, we demonstrate that different aspects of linguistic structure are learned at different rates, with part of speech tagging acquired early and global topic information learned continuously.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: Triangulation as an Acceptance Rule for Multilingual Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we validate mechanistic explanations for multilingual models to ensure they are causal and invariant across languages and scripts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces triangulation, an acceptance rule for mechanistic interpretability that requires necessity, sufficiency, and invariance across predicate-preserving environments to filter spurious circuits.
papers.conclusion: Triangulation offers a concrete step toward rigorous, transferable mechanistic explanations by requiring cross-environment consistency, allowing circuits that pass to be interpreted with greater confidence as capturing language-agnostic mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.
Triangulation can be extended to multimodal settings by holding the image fixed and varying the prompt language.
Triangulation enables separation of circuits into visual, linguistic, and spurious categories based on cross-environment invariance.
The method is grounded in causal abstraction theory and provides an approximate transformation score over interchange interventions.
Triangulation requires explicit cue-only falsifiers to reject mechanisms that rely on surface cues rather than predicate information.
papers.limitation:
Multiple circuits may satisfy triangulation if their effects are redundant; triangulation identifies sufficient mechanisms but does not guarantee uniqueness.
The quality of reference families is decisive, and poor-quality families can mislead by either accepting spurious circuits or rejecting genuine circuits.
Causal interventions at scale are computationally expensive, and prioritization strategies are advisable for practical deployment.
When using LLM judges to verify predicate preservation, circularity risks arise if the judge correlates with the model under study.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models achieve strong aggregate performance yet often behave unpredictably across languages, scripts, and cultures. We argue that mechanistic explanations for such models should satisfy a \emph{causal} standard: claims must survive causal interventions and must \emph{cross-reference} across environments that perturb surface form while preserving meaning. We formalize \emph{reference families} as predicate-preserving variants and introduce \emph{triangulation}, an acceptance rule requiring necessity (ablating the circuit degrades the target behavior), sufficiency (patching activations transfers the behavior), and invariance (both effects remain directionally stable and of sufficient magnitude across the reference family). To supply candidate subgraphs, we adopt automatic circuit discovery and \emph{accept or reject} those candidates by triangulation. We ground triangulation in causal abstraction by casting it as an approximate transformation score over a distribution of interchange interventions, connect it to the pragmatic interpretability agenda, and present a comparative experimental protocol across multiple model families, language pairs, and tasks. Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.

papers.title: How Distributed are Distributed Representations? An Observation on the Locality of Syntactic Information in Verb Agreement Tasks
papers.research_question: Where is syntactic information localized in transformer representations for French object-past participle agreement tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Syntactic information is encoded locally in transformer representations in a way consistent with French grammar, as shown through probing and causal analysis.
papers.conclusion: Transformers process French object-past participle agreement in a linguistically-motivated manner, and this work is a step towards understanding inner representations.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic information is encoded locally within context tokens and not distributed globally across the sentence.
Masking linguistically relevant tokens (antecedent and relative pronoun) degrades prediction performance, indicating a causal link.
Number information is encoded in a small number of dimensions but redundantly across the representation.
Probing accuracy is high in context tokens and drops in prefix and suffix, showing localized encoding.
Transformers rely on tokens consistent with French grammar for agreement prediction.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a specific linguistic phenomenon (object-past participle agreement) in French and could be extended to other languages and phenomena.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other linguistic phenomena and languages.
papers.abstract: This work addresses the question of the localization of syntactic information encoded in the transformers representations. We tackle this question from two perspectives, considering the object-past participle agreement in French, by identifying, first, in which part of the sentence and, second, in which part of the representation syntactic information is encoded. The results of our experiments using probing, causal analysis and feature selection method, show that syntactic information is encoded locally in a way consistent with the French grammar.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: Concept Space Alignment in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: Is there a linear mapping between corresponding concepts in different languages in multilingual LLMs, and how does a learned linear mapping generalize to new concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs exhibit high-quality linear concept alignment across languages, but prompt-based embeddings break some of the implicit alignment and generalize worse, especially for typologically distant languages and physical concepts.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs exhibit high-quality, linear concept alignment across different languages, but the ability of supervised maps to generalize varied across different models, languages, and ways of obtaining embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models exhibit very high-quality linear alignments between corresponding concepts in different languages.
Prompt-based embeddings align less linearly than vanilla word embeddings, indicating that some implicitly learned alignments are broken by prompting.
Generalization works best for languages with similar typology (Indo-European) and for abstract concepts.
Abstract concepts exhibit better alignment than physical concepts, which is explained by their higher frequency in training data.
The degree of isomorphism to English is similar across languages, but induced maps generalize much better across typologically related languages.
papers.limitation:
Only six test languages are included due to small overlap between multilingual WordNets, which is too small to draw universally applicable conclusions.
The study is limited to nouns; it is unclear how linear alignment generalizes to other parts of speech.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) seem to generalize somewhat across languages. We hypothesize this is a result of implicit vector space alignment. Evaluating such alignment, we see that larger models exhibit very high-quality linear alignments between corresponding concepts in different languages. Our experiments show that multilingual LLMs suffer from two familiar weaknesses: generalization works best for languages with similar typology, and for abstract concepts. For some models, e.g., the Llama-2 family of models, prompt-based embeddings align better than word embeddings, but the projections are less linear -- an observation that holds across almost all model families, indicating that some of the implicitly learned alignments are broken somewhat by prompt-based methods.

papers.title: LinguaLens: Towards Interpreting Linguistic Mechanisms of Large Language Models via Sparse Auto-Encoder
papers.research_question: Can we identify the minimal components within an LLM responsible for specific linguistic processing abilities? Can we comprehensively model the internal linguistic functionalities of the model?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LINGUALENS, a framework using Sparse Auto-Encoders to interpret linguistic mechanisms in LLMs, revealing intrinsic representations of linguistic knowledge, cross-layer and cross-lingual distribution patterns, and enabling control of model outputs.
papers.conclusion: LINGUALENS provides a systematic framework for interpreting linguistic mechanisms in LLMs, showing that they encode structured linguistic knowledge and enabling more interpretable and controllable language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
LINGUALENS effectively identifies linguistic features in SAE space, with metrics like FRC showing strong correlations.
Linguistic functions distribute across layers in stages: morphology and syntax in lower layers, pragmatics in middle layers, and deep semantics in upper layers.
Cross-lingual analysis shows higher overlap for semantic and pragmatic features than morphological and syntactic ones, indicating shared representations.
Interventions on SAE features (ablation and enhancement) demonstrate causal effects on model outputs, validated by LLM judges.
Deep semantics processing, such as reference resolution and metaphor interpretation, activates specific base vectors in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Dataset size is limited to approximately 50 sentence pairs per linguistic feature.
Feature count is 145, which is not comprehensive for all linguistic phenomena.
Experiments are conducted only on Llama-3.1-8B due to computational constraints.
Intervention effects are less stable and efficacious compared to conventional fine-tuning techniques.
future_direction: Expand the dataset to include more linguistic features and sentences.
Apply the framework to a wider variety of model architectures and larger models.
Refine SAE-based intervention methods for better efficacy and stability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on tasks requiring complex linguistic abilities, such as reference disambiguation and metaphor recognition/generation. Although LLMs possess impressive capabilities, their internal mechanisms for processing and representing linguistic knowledge remain largely opaque. Prior research on linguistic mechanisms is limited by coarse granularity, limited analysis scale, and narrow focus. In this study, we propose LinguaLens, a systematic and comprehensive framework for analyzing the linguistic mechanisms of large language models, based on Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs). We extract a broad set of Chinese and English linguistic features across four dimensions (morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics). By employing counterfactual methods, we construct a large-scale counterfactual dataset of linguistic features for mechanism analysis. Our findings reveal intrinsic representations of linguistic knowledge in LLMs, uncover patterns of cross-layer and cross-lingual distribution, and demonstrate the potential to control model outputs. This work provides a systematic suite of resources and methods for studying linguistic mechanisms, offers strong evidence that LLMs possess genuine linguistic knowledge, and lays the foundation for more interpretable and controllable language modeling in future research.

papers.title: The Stem Cell Hypothesis: Dilemma behind Multi-Task Learning with Transformer Encoders
papers.research_question: Why does multi-task learning (MTL) with transformer encoders on distinct core NLP tasks lead to worse performance than single-task learning, and is there a subset of attention heads that are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for all?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Stem Cell Hypothesis, which states that a subset of attention heads (stem cells) are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks, leading to interference and worse performance in multi-task learning.
papers.conclusion: The Stem Cell Hypothesis sheds light on the dilemma of multi-task learning with transformer encoders, indicating that attention heads cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks without interference, and suggests a direction for future MTL research by wisely assigning heads to tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task learning on five core NLP tasks (POS, NER, DEP, CON, SRL) results in lower performance than single-task learning for all tasks.
Pruning analysis reveals that all five tasks rely on a similar set of attention heads, primarily in middle layers (5-8), which are termed 'stem cells'.
Even without fine-tuning, certain attention heads (stem cells) show high probing accuracy for specific linguistic labels, demonstrating their pluripotency.
During single-task learning, stem cells become specialized for the task, but during multi-task learning, they lose specialization due to conflicting training signals.
The Stem Cell Hypothesis is validated by novel parameter-free probes that show how attention heads are transformed during training, with MTL often degrading probing and task performance.
future_direction: Adapt the work to more tasks and languages for broader generality.
Design another probing method for deeper analysis in constituency parsing (CON).
papers.abstract: Multi-task learning with transformer encoders (MTL) has emerged as a powerful technique to improve performance on closely-related tasks for both accuracy and efficiency while a question still remains whether or not it would perform as well on tasks that are distinct in nature. We first present MTL results on five NLP tasks, POS, NER, DEP, CON, and SRL, and depict its deficiency over single-task learning. We then conduct an extensive pruning analysis to show that a certain set of attention heads get claimed by most tasks during MTL, who interfere with one another to fine-tune those heads for their own objectives. Based on this finding, we propose the Stem Cell Hypothesis to reveal the existence of attention heads naturally talented for many tasks that cannot be jointly trained to create adequate embeddings for all of those tasks. Finally, we design novel parameter-free probes to justify our hypothesis and demonstrate how attention heads are transformed across the five tasks during MTL through label analysis. papers.title: Large Language Models Are Partially Primed in Pronoun Interpretation
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) adapt their referential biases in pronoun interpretation in a human-like way when exposed to consistent referential patterns in the local discourse context?
papers.core_contribution: InstructGPT can adapt its syntactic bias in pronoun interpretation from exposure to referential patterns in the local context, but fails to adapt its semantic bias, suggesting LLMs only partially represent semantic knowledge in referential processing.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can adapt to syntactic patterns in pronoun interpretation from local exposure, but not to semantic patterns, indicating a partial and non-human-like representation of semantic knowledge in referential processing.
papers.key_findings:
InstructGPT adapted its syntactic bias (subject vs. non-subject preference) based on recent exposure, showing sensitivity to syntactic patterns in the local discourse.
InstructGPT exhibited a strong, persistent goal bias in pronoun interpretation that was not influenced by exposure to source/goal patterns, unlike human participants.
FLAN-UL2 failed to generate meaningful patterns, answering 'yes' 100% of the time to ambiguous target questions and showing poor comprehension.
The adaptation to syntactic patterns was observed even in the presence of confounding semantic goal bias (Experiment 2a).
The results suggest LLMs may over-represent semantic knowledge (goal bias) or lack the ability to track and adapt to higher-level semantic pattern frequencies across a discourse.
papers.limitation:
The study simulated participants only by manipulating the temperature hyperparameter; more sophisticated prompting methods could be explored.
Direct comparison with psycholinguistic experiments might not be the only method to investigate LLMs' discourse capacity.
The study is strictly behavioral and does not analyze the models' internal representations.
future_direction: Incorporate more detailed prompting to simulate diverse linguistic backgrounds in experimental simulations.
Mitigate the semantic knowledge gap via instruction fine-tuning or chain-of-thought prompting.
Explore a comprehensive list of discourse probing tasks as an alternative method.
papers.abstract: While a large body of literature suggests that large language models (LLMs) acquire rich linguistic representations, little is known about whether they adapt to linguistic biases in a human-like way. The present study probes this question by asking whether LLMs display human-like referential biases using stimuli and procedures from real psycholinguistic experiments. Recent psycholinguistic studies suggest that humans adapt their referential biases with recent exposure to referential patterns; closely replicating three relevant psycholinguistic experiments from Johnson & Arnold (2022) in an in-context learning (ICL) framework, we found that InstructGPT adapts its pronominal interpretations in response to the frequency of referential patterns in the local discourse, though in a limited fashion: adaptation was only observed relative to syntactic but not semantic biases. By contrast, FLAN-UL2 fails to generate meaningful patterns. Our results provide further evidence that contemporary LLMs discourse representations are sensitive to syntactic patterns in the local context but less so to semantic patterns. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/zkx06111/llm_priming.

papers.title: The Other Mind: How Language Models Exhibit Human Temporal Cognition
papers.research_question: How do large language models exhibit human-like temporal cognition, specifically whether they spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs spontaneously exhibit human-like temporal cognition, establishing a subjective reference point and adhering to the Weber-Fechner law, which emerges from multi-level convergence at neuronal, representational, and informational levels.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit human-like temporal cognition through multi-level convergence, suggesting cognition is a subjective construction of the external world. This points to the risk of alien cognitive frameworks and the need for AI alignment paradigms that guide internal world-building.
papers.key_findings:
In similarity judgment tasks, larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point (ca. 2025) and their perception of time logarithmically compresses as years recede from this point, adhering to the Weber-Fechner law.
A subgroup of temporal-preferential neurons in the FFN exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme similar to biological systems.
Representations of years undergo hierarchical construction: from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation organized around a reference point in deep layers.
Pre-trained embedding models reveal that the training corpus possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, providing raw material for the model's internal construction of temporal cognition.
The findings support an experientialist perspective where LLM cognition is a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system, leading to potential convergence with or divergence from human cognition.
future_direction: Evolve AI alignment beyond behavioral control to a paradigm that actively guides the formation of a model's internal world from its source.
Monitor models' emergent representational and cognitive patterns and enable intervention across the chain of cognition.
Curate the AI's environment with harmless or formalized verifiable information exposures.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, they exhibit certain cognitive patterns similar to those of humans that are not directly specified in training data. This study investigates this phenomenon by focusing on temporal cognition in LLMs. Leveraging the similarity judgment task, we find that larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law, whereby the perceived distance logarithmically compresses as years recede from this reference point. To uncover the mechanisms behind this behavior, we conducted multiple analyses across neuronal, representational, and informational levels. We first identify a set of temporal-preferential neurons and find that this group exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme convergently found in biological systems. Probing representations of years reveals a hierarchical construction process, where years evolve from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation in deep layers. Finally, using pre-trained embedding models, we found that the training corpus itself possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, which provides the raw material for the model's internal construction. In discussion, we propose an experientialist perspective for understanding these findings, where the LLMs' cognition is viewed as a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system. This nuanced perspective implies the potential emergence of alien cognitive frameworks that humans cannot intuitively predict, pointing toward a direction for AI alignment that focuses on guiding internal constructions. Our code is available at https://TheOtherMind.github.io.

papers.title: Probing for Understanding of English Verb Classes and Alternations in Large Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Do PLM word-level representations encode information about which syntactic frames an individual verb can participate in? At the sentence level, do PLM embeddings encode the frame-selectional properties of their main verb?
papers.core_contribution: PLM contextual embeddings encode linguistic information about verb alternation classes at both the word and sentence level, with middle-to-upper layers achieving better performance than lower layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results support the hypothesis that PLM contextual embeddings encode linguistic information about verb alternation classes at both the word and sentence level.
papers.key_findings:
PLM embeddings significantly outperform non-contextual embeddings (e.g., GloVe) on verb alternation class prediction tasks.
Middle-to-upper layers of PLMs encode more information about verb alternation classes than lower layers, as shown by higher probing performance.
ELECTRA performs best on the sentence-level acceptability judgment task, potentially due to its pre-training task resembling the acceptability judgment task.
Linear probes are sufficiently selective for the word-level task, as demonstrated by control experiments.
Performance varies across different verb alternation classes and across different PLM architectures.
papers.limitation:
Only five alternation classes are analyzed, which is a small subset of the 83 classes presented in Levin (1993).
The control task ensures the classifier probe is selective for the first experiment and BERT, but it may not generalize well to the second experiment, other syntactic frames, and other models.
future_direction: Test whether the insights extend to the dozens of alternations described in Levin (1993) that are not present in the LaVA and FAVA datasets.
Analyze small and large variants of the PLMs to directly evaluate the effect of scaling training data and model size.
Use alternative probing approaches like unsupervised evaluation of minimal pairs or 'amnesic probing' to mitigate the risk of probes picking up arbitrary signals.
papers.abstract: We investigate the extent to which verb alternation classes, as described by Levin (1993), are encoded in the embeddings of Large Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) such as BERT, RoBERTa, ELECTRA, and DeBERTa using selectively constructed diagnostic classifiers for word and sentence-level prediction tasks. We follow and expand upon the experiments of Kann et al. (2019), which aim to probe whether static embeddings encode frame-selectional properties of verbs. At both the word and sentence level, we find that contextual embeddings from PLMs not only outperform non-contextual embeddings, but achieve astonishingly high accuracies on tasks across most alternation classes. Additionally, we find evidence that the middle-to-upper layers of PLMs achieve better performance on average than the lower layers across all probing tasks.

papers.title: Morph Call: Probing Morphosyntactic Content of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: What morphosyntactic knowledge do multilingual transformer models encode, and how does fine-tuning for POS-tagging affect this knowledge?
